lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6, which part of a computer runs a program's instructions? (The processor, or CPU.) Today: how the processor runs a program, one instruction at a time.
A program is stored in memory as instructions, each at a numbered place called an address. Its data is in memory too. John von Neumann (1903-1957) described this stored-program idea in 1945.
The processor repeats a cycle billions of times a second. Fetch: get the next instruction from memory. Decode: work out what it means. Execute: do it. Then fetch the next one.

Inside the processor, the control unit runs the cycle, and the ALU (arithmetic logic unit) does sums and comparisons. Registers are tiny fast stores: the program counter holds the next instruction's address.
Worked example: LOAD 7 puts 7 in the accumulator. ADD 5 makes it 7 + 5 = 12. OUT shows 12. HALT stops. Each one is fetched, decoded and executed, and the program counter moves on: 0, 1, 2, 3.

Machine code is these instructions as binary numbers, all the processor understands. People write text code, and a translator turns it into machine code: a compiler all at once, an interpreter line by line.
Clock speed counts cycles: 1 hertz is 1 a second, so a 3 gigahertz (GHz) processor runs 3 billion cycles a second. A processor with several cores can run several instructions at the same time.

Try it in the world: act the cycle out with a friend. One is the memory, holding numbered cards; the other is the processor, who fetches a card, reads it aloud and does it. Next: text, sound and pictures as bits.

exercises.prompt: Put the processor's cycle in order, from the start.
exercises.hint: The cycle's name gives its order.
exercises.explain: Fetch, decode, execute, and round again with the next instruction.

exercises.prompt: Match each part to its job.
exercises.hint: Think of what each name says.
exercises.explain: The control unit runs the cycle, the ALU calculates, the program counter points to the next instruction and memory stores programs and data.

exercises.prompt: Which part does sums and comparisons?
exercises.hint: Its name has arithmetic and logic in it.
exercises.explain: The ALU, the arithmetic logic unit, does the sums and the comparisons.

exercises.prompt: A 3 GHz processor runs 3 billion cycles a second.
exercises.hint: Giga means a billion, and hertz means each second.
exercises.explain: True: 1 GHz is a billion cycles each second, so 3 GHz is 3 billion.

exercises.prompt: This program runs. What number does OUT show?
exercises.hint: Keep the accumulator's value as each line runs.
exercises.explain: LOAD 9 puts 9 in the accumulator; ADD 4 makes 9 + 4 = 13; OUT shows 13.

exercises.prompt: This program runs. What number does OUT show?
exercises.hint: Write the accumulator's value after every line.

exercises.prompt: An instruction has just been executed. What happens next?
exercises.hint: The processor goes round a cycle.
exercises.explain: It goes round the cycle again: the next instruction is fetched, decoded and executed.

exercises.prompt: Machine code is binary numbers that the processor understands.
exercises.hint: Think what the processor reads in the end.
exercises.explain: True: every program becomes machine code, binary instructions the processor fetches and executes.

exercises.prompt: Where is it: stored in memory, or a part of the processor?
exercises.hint: Is it something stored, or something that works?
exercises.explain: Programs and data are stored in memory; the ALU, the control unit and the registers such as the program counter are inside the processor.

choices: turns a whole program into machine code first
runs one line, then translates the next
exercises.explain: A compiler translates the whole program before it runs; an interpreter translates and runs it a line at a time.

exercises.prompt: A processor runs at 2 GHz. How many billion cycles does it run in 5 seconds?
exercises.hint: GHz means billions of cycles each second.
exercises.explain: 2 billion cycles a second for 5 seconds: 2 × 5 = 10 billion.

exercises.prompt: How many instructions does this program fetch and execute, counting HALT?
exercises.hint: Follow the program counter from address 0 until HALT.
exercises.explain: It runs every instruction once, from LOAD 5 at address 0 to HALT at address 5: 6 instructions.

exercises.prompt: What number does the second OUT show?
exercises.hint: Keep the accumulator's value line by line, and count the OUTs.
exercises.explain: 12 − 5 = 7, so the first OUT shows 7; then 7 + 10 = 17, and the second OUT shows 17.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between an interpreter and a compiler?
choices: an interpreter translates a line at a time
a compiler works only on short programs
a compiler runs code without a processor
exercises.hint: Think of when each one translates.
exercises.explain: An interpreter translates and runs one line at a time; a compiler translates the whole program first.

exercises.prompt: A processor with 4 cores can run instructions for 4 tasks at the same time.
exercises.hint: Each core has a fetch-decode-execute cycle of its own.
exercises.explain: True: each core fetches, decodes and executes its own instructions, so 4 can work at once.

exercises.prompt: Why is it useful that programs and data share the same memory?
choices: new programs load with no rewiring
exercises.hint: Think of the first computers, which were rewired for each job.
exercises.explain: With programs stored in memory like data, a computer runs a new program just by loading it.
